newsitem.title: USA: Viacom stock tumbles on Blockbuster worries.
newsitem.headline: Viacom stock tumbles on Blockbuster worries.

text.p: Viacom Inc's stock slid to a year low on Tuesday as Wall Street grew increasingly worried that the company's troubles with its Blockbuster unit were far from over.

The company's projections that operating cash flow would be down between 15 percent and 20 percent -- coupled with the resignation of the unit's chairman and chief executive, Bill Fields -- were what worried investors, analysts said.
Viacom also said Tuesday it planned to issue separately traded shares of Blockbuster by early 1998, with the proceeds going to pay off debt.

It also said that it expects Blockbuster's first quarter earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization to be down between 15 percent and 20 percent because of "inferior quality of video releases in the period,"
In early afternoon trading, the company's stock had dropped 5-1/4 to 25-3/4, below the 52-week low of 29-3/4. By early afternoon, more than two million shares had been traded.
Several analysts said that projection was particularly troubling since they only recently lowered their estimates for Viacom, largely because of sluggish business at Blockbuster.

"It's just disappointing that within a couple-week period, the numbers are coming down yet again," said Merrill Lynch analyst Jessica Reif. "It just questions the company's ability to effectively budget or know what's going on in the business."
Viacom also announced that Fields, Blockbuster's chairman and chief executive, was resigning. No replacement was named, but Viacom said it expected to announce its selection shortly.
"Bill Fields was presented as the savior. Now the savior is dead. He fell on his sword," said Josephthal Lyon & Ross analyst Dennis McAlpine.
A spokeswoman would not say if Viacom was looking to candidates inside or outside the company.
Fields, a former Wal-Mart Stores Inc executive, said he wanted to return to general retailing.
Fields joined Blockbuster in March 1996, succeeding Steve Berrard, who had close ties to Wayne Huizenga, the businessman who built Blockbuster and left shortly after its 1994 merger with Viacom.
Several analysts said they were concerned since it will likely take Fields' successor at least 12 months to get up to speed with the unit's operations, potentially stalling any turnaround.
"So we have to restart the clock there," Reif said.
Blockbuster has been a difficult segment for Viacom as the cable and satellite industries cut into the video retailing.
The company said it considered several alternatives for Blockbuster, including a spinoff of the unit.
Viacom has about $9.9 billion in debt, a company spokeswoman said. Its planned sale of 10 radio stations is expected to lower the debt by between $700 million and $800 million.
Viacom on Tuesday repeated its goal to lower debt to between $6 billion and $8 billion by the end of 1999.
"Blockbuster continues to deteriorate and that's obviously troubling," said Smith Barney analyst Jill Krutick.
At the end of 1996, Blockbuster comprised more than 5,300 U.S. and international video stores and about 500 music stores.

Its Blockbuster video and music store operations reported revenues of $3.54 billion and EBITDA of $775 million in 1996. For the 1996 year, Viacom reported revenues of $12.08 billion and EBITDA of $2.09 billion.
